t.2.42.1: Of the city-dwellers who had followed Rāma and then turned back, dispirited, it was as though their very life-breaths had departed.
t.2.42.2: Having returned each to his own home, surrounded by their sons and wives, they all shed tears, their faces covered with weeping.
t.2.42.3: No one rejoiced, nor did the merchants take delight or spread out their wares; the goods no longer looked attractive, and the householders did not cook.
t.2.42.4: People did not rejoice on seeing again what had been lost, nor at a large gain of wealth; and a mother, having obtained her firstborn son, did not rejoice.
t.2.42.5: In house after house the weeping women, stricken with grief, reproached each husband who had come home, wounding him with words as elephants are driven with goads.
t.2.42.7: Lakṣmaṇa alone is the one truly good man in the world, he who, together with Sītā, follows Rāma, the Kākutstha, into the forest, serving him there.
t.2.42.8: Blessed with merit are those rivers, the lotus ponds and the lakes in which Kākutstha will bathe, plunging into their pure water.
t.2.42.9: The forests with their lovely groves, the rivers with their broad marshy banks, and the mountains with their ridges will adorn Kākutstha.
t.2.42.10: Whatever forest or mountain Rāma goes to, they will not be able to keep from honoring him when he arrives, as one honors a beloved guest.
t.2.42.11: The mountains, crowned with garlands of many-colored flowers and bearing abundant clusters of blossoms, will out of compassion display their choicest flowers and fruits even out of season to Rāma when he has come.
t.2.42.6: What use, indeed, have they for houses, what for wives, or what for wealth? What use for sons, or even for pleasures, those who do not see Rāghava?
t.2.42.12: The trees on the mountain peaks, showing him again and again many kinds of bright and wondrous waterfalls, will delight Rāghava.
t.2.42.13: Where Rāma is, there is no fear here, nor is there any defeat there; for he is a hero, mighty-armed, and the son of Daśaratha.
t.2.42.14: Before he goes far from us, let us follow Rāghava; pleasant is the shade at the feet of such a great-souled master. For he is the protector of these people, he is their refuge, he is their final resort.
t.2.42.15: "We shall attend upon Sītā, while you attend upon Rāghava": so the women of the city, afflicted with grief, said this and that to their husbands.
t.2.42.16: In the forest Rāghava will provide for your welfare and security; Sītā will see to the welfare and security of these womenfolk.
t.2.42.17: Who indeed could take delight in this cheerless and unlovely dwelling, whose people are filled with longing and whose heart has been stolen away?
t.2.42.18: If the kingdom should become Kaikeyī's, unrighteous and as though without a protector, then we have no use for life itself; what use have we for sons, what use for wealth?
t.2.42.19: She by whom both son and husband were cast off for the sake of sovereignty, that Kaikeyī, the disgrace of her family, whom else would she spare?
t.2.42.21: She who, pitiless, drives into exile the son of the lord of kings, that unrighteous woman of wicked conduct, who, having gained her, could live happily?
t.2.42.20: Never, so long as we live, shall we dwell as servants in the kingdom of Kaikeyī while she lives; this we swear even by our sons.
t.2.42.22: For with Rāma gone into exile, the lord of the earth will surely not live; and once Daśaratha is dead, ruin will clearly follow immediately after.
t.2.42.23: You, whose merit is exhausted and who are utterly wretched, stir up poison and drink it! Or follow Rāghava, or else go away where you will never be heard of again!
t.2.42.24: Rāma has been wrongfully banished, together with his wife and with Lakṣmaṇa, and we have been handed over to Bharata like beasts to a butcher.
t.2.42.25: Lamenting thus in the city, those women of the city, sorely afflicted, cried out aloud, as if at the approach of the terror of death.
t.2.42.26: The women, distressed on account of Rāma, lamented and wept, wretched and senseless, as though a son or a brother had been banished; for he had been dearer to them even than their own sons.
